parts: Take a one-dollar bill out of your wallet.
Turn it over.
An eye floats above a pyramid.
For decades, people have said a secret brotherhood put it there.
And it is not alone.
There is a brain people see in a Vatican ceiling.
A ritual in an opera.
A secret in a Scottish chapel.
Four cases.
One has a paper trail.
One is still argued over by experts.
One breaks the calendar.
And one involves a plant that seems out of place in a Scottish chapel.
Which of these are real?
Here are the rules.
For every case, we will look at the paper trail.
Names.
Dates.
Records.
Then we stamp it.
Documented means the records exist.
Disputed means experts still argue.
Myth means the dates, or the evidence, say no.
And when a conclusion is ours and not a historian's, we will call it our reading.
Let's start with the bill.
The story starts in July seventeen seventy-six.
Congress asks Franklin, Jefferson and Adams for a seal for the new country.
A second committee tries in seventeen eighty.
Then a third.
It takes six years.
The eye comes first, in a glowing triangle, from an artist, Pierre Du Simitière.
The pyramid comes later, from a heraldry expert, William Barton, in seventeen eighty-two.
Then the secretary of Congress, Charles Thomson, stitches the ideas together.
Congress approves his design on June twentieth, seventeen eighty-two.
A committee, an artist, an expert, a secretary.
So where are the Masons?
Now the eye.
It was not a Masonic invention.
Religious art had used an eye inside a triangle for the Trinity.
The artist who proposed it for the seal, Du Simitière, was not a Mason.
Masonic handbooks show the eye as a standard symbol only in the seventeen nineties.
Years after the seal.
And among that first committee, only one is known to have been a Mason.
Benjamin Franklin.
So how did it reach your wallet?
In nineteen thirty-four, the Secretary of Agriculture, Henry Wallace, reads a history of the seal.
He loves the motto, Novus Ordo Seclorum, a new order of the ages.
He later said it matched the New Deal.
He suggests putting the seal on a coin.
President Roosevelt prefers the one-dollar bill.
And here is the twist.
Roosevelt really was a Freemason, since nineteen eleven. We found no record he chose the design for that.
But the seal was finished.
A hundred and fifty-three years before that bill.
The dollar of nineteen thirty-five is the first with both sides of the seal.
Verdict.
The design story is documented.
The idea that Masons created it is a myth.
Case two.
Rome, fifteen oh eight to fifteen twelve.
Michelangelo paints the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
In nineteen ninety, a medical journal, JAMA, publishes an idea.
The shape around God in The Creation of Adam looks like a human brain.
In twenty ten, a neurosurgery journal goes further.
It proposes a brain stem in God's neck, in another panel.
Under that reading, God gives Adam more than life.
He gives intelligence.
And Michelangelo really did study anatomy up close.
His biographer Condivi wrote about it in fifteen fifty-three.
But hold on.
Other readers look at the same neck and see a goiter.
Others see a womb in the red cloak, and an umbilical cord in the green scarf.
Skeptics ask a classic question: do we see a pattern because it is there, or because we want to?
It is the man in the moon.
Verdict.
The brain is disputed.
Nobody can prove what Michelangelo meant.
We found no document where he says so.
Now a bolder rumor, one we could not trace to a source: could the ceiling hide a Masonic code?
Check the calendar.
Michelangelo died in fifteen sixty-four.
Lodge records appear only in the late fifteen hundreds, and the first Grand Lodge was founded in seventeen seventeen.
A hundred and fifty-three years later.
The same gap as the dollar.
Coincidence, not code.
We found no record that connects Michelangelo to any lodge.
A Masonic message on that ceiling would need a time machine.
Verdict: myth.
Case three has a happy kind of proof.
Vienna, December fourteenth, seventeen eighty-four.
A composer is initiated into a Masonic lodge called Beneficence.
His name is Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart.
Within weeks, he moves up a degree.
Within months, he is a Master Mason.
In seventeen eighty-five, his father Leopold joins too.
Mozart writes mourning music for two lodge brothers who have died.
And in November seventeen ninety-one, he completes a Masonic cantata for the opening of a temple.
Often called his last completed work.
A few weeks earlier, on September thirtieth, seventeen ninety-one, a new opera opens in Vienna.
The librettist himself, Emanuel Schikaneder, leads the company.
It is called The Magic Flute.
Now listen for the pattern.
The overture opens with three solemn chords.
Three ladies.
Three boys.
Three temples.
The heroes face trials of silence, fire and water, which scholars compare to initiation rites.
But careful.
Three-chord openings also appear in operas that are not Masonic at all.
And the story mixes fairy tale, Egypt, Enlightenment and folk comedy.
Verdict.
Mozart's Freemasonry is documented.
How much of the opera is Masonic is disputed.
Our reading: a real hidden message leaves a paper trail.
The dollar bill has a committee and a vote.
The ceiling has no lodge at all.
Mozart has a lodge, a date, and a score.
Keep that thought, because the last case has almost no paper.
It has stone.
Case four.
A small chapel south of Edinburgh, in Scotland.
Rosslyn Chapel.
Work began in the mid-fourteen hundreds, for Sir William Sinclair.
And there is a rumor: a hidden Templar secret.
The Knights Templar were dissolved by the pope in thirteen twelve.
Historians say the Templar link has no basis.
The chapel was founded so that Masses would be said for the dead, including the Sinclair family.
Verdict on the Templars: myth.
Then there is the Masonic link, and this one is real.
In seventeen thirty-six, William St Clair of Roslin, from the Rosslyn family, was elected the first Grand Master Mason of Scotland.
Documented.
But that is nearly three centuries after the chapel began.
Now the plant.
On an arch in the south aisle, there is a carving that looks like ears of corn.
The chapel's own website says it appears to be maize.
Maize comes from the Americas.
The chapel was begun decades before Columbus sailed in fourteen ninety-two.
If it is maize, someone had seen it before Columbus.
But some experts doubt it.
Some experts read these shapes as stylised patterns.
A pattern can look like corn without being corn.
Verdict: disputed.
Three things could settle it.
Compare the carvings with real plants.
Separate what is medieval from what was restored in the eighteen sixties.
Find written records of the builders.
Until then, nobody can prove it.
There is one thing we can prove.
At L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, archaeologists found wood cut with metal tools.
In twenty twenty-one, a study in Nature read the tree rings.
A radiocarbon spike from the year nine ninety-three worked like a clock.
The best fit for when the trees were cut: the year ten twenty-one.
Norse explorers had reached Newfoundland about four hundred and seventy years before Columbus.
That crossing is documented.
And it tells us nothing about Rosslyn.
So, back to your wallet.
The dollar bill: a committee, an artist, a secretary, and a Masonic myth.
The Sistine ceiling: a disputed brain, and a Masonic code that fails on the calendar.
Mozart: documented, with a lodge and a date.
Rosslyn: a Templar myth, a late but documented Masonic link, and a disputed plant.
Our reading: the real ones leave a paper trail.
The rest usually add the secret society later.
So when someone says hidden message, ask one question.
Where is the paper?
One more question.
Why is the dollar green?
